terms: From 2026, the front and rear wings move between two settings during a lap: corner mode (wings closed, full downforce) and straight mode (wings opened on designated straights to cut drag). It is available to every driver on every lap, unlike DRS.
The low-drag active-aero setting used from 2026: front and rear wing flaps open on designated straights to raise top speed. Early drafts of the rules called it X-mode.
The default high-downforce active-aero setting from 2026, with the wings closed for cornering grip. Early drafts of the rules called it Z-mode.
A scaffold-like metal grid of pressure sensors (pitot tubes) bolted to a car in testing or practice to measure the airflow behind the wheels, wings or floor.
Complex vanes between the front wheels and the sidepods that steered the turbulent wake of the front tyres away from the floor. Effectively banned by the 2022 rules.
A small lower wing element below the main rear wing that works with the diffuser to pull air out from under the car.
When the underside of the car (the plank and its titanium skid blocks) strikes the track, usually at high speed or over bumps, throwing sparks.
Undisturbed air in front of a car with nobody close ahead. A car in clean air has its full downforce and cooling.
The hot, turbulent wake behind a car. A driver following closely loses downforce, slides more and overheats tyres and brakes, which makes overtaking harder.
The tendency of a gas jet to follow a curved surface. Around 2012–2013 teams used it to bend hot exhaust gases down toward the diffuser for extra downforce.
The upswept rear section of the floor. It lets the fast air from under the car slow and expand, which keeps pressure under the car low and sucks it onto the track.
A loophole of 2009 in which Brawn, Toyota and Williams built a second diffuser deck for extra downforce. Banned from 2011.
Using exhaust gas blown through the diffuser to add downforce, even off the throttle by keeping the engine firing. Peaked with Red Bull in 2011; restricted from 2012.
Aerodynamic load pushing the car down onto the track. More downforce means more grip and faster cornering, at the cost of more drag.
Aerodynamic resistance slowing the car down, most noticeable on straights.

Drag Reduction System, used from 2011 to 2025: an opening flap in the rear wing (up to 85 mm) that a driver within one second of the car ahead at a detection point could use in designated zones. Replaced by active aero and overtake mode in 2026.
A designated straight where DRS could be opened, with a detection point before it (2011–2025).
The vertical panel at each end of a wing, managing the vortices that form where high- and low-pressure air meet.
The underside of the car. Since 2022 it produces most of the downforce through shaped Venturi tunnels.
Fluorescent paint (usually paraffin-based) sprayed on the bodywork in practice. Air streaks the paint as it dries, showing engineers how the flow moves over the car.
The wing at the nose. It creates front downforce and shapes the airflow for the rest of the car.
Producing downforce mainly from the underside of the car, with shaped tunnels creating low pressure beneath it. First used in F1 by Lotus in 1977–78, banned in 1983 and brought back in 2022.
A small vertical lip on the trailing edge of a wing that adds a lot of downforce for little drag. Named after Dan Gurney.
The titanium cockpit protection hoop above the driver's head, compulsory since 2018. It must withstand about 125 kN, roughly 12 tonnes.
The carbon-fibre survival cell that holds the driver and fuel tank, built to stay intact in heavy impacts.
Bodywork designed to push the front-tyre wake outward, away from the floor. The 2022 rules were written to reduce it; inwash directs air inward instead.
A 10 mm wood-composite board under the car that enforces a minimum ride height. If it is worn by more than 1 mm the car is disqualified.
Violent bouncing at speed on ground-effect cars: the floor gets so close to the track that the airflow stalls, the car pops up, regains downforce and is sucked down again.
The nose-down, tail-up stance of a car. High-rake cars (Red Bull before 2022) turned the whole floor into a bigger diffuser.
The distance between the floor and the track. Lower usually means more downforce, until the car starts bottoming or porpoising.
The bodywork on each side of the cockpit, holding the radiators and side-impact structures and shaping air toward the rear.
Running close behind another car on a straight, where the car ahead has punched a hole in the air. The follower has less drag and gains speed.
A spinning tube of air created on purpose by wing tips or floor edges, used to seal the low pressure under the car. The Y250 vortex came off the middle of the pre-2022 front wing.
The shaped channels under the floor of the post-2022 cars that speed up the air and generate ground-effect downforce.
A 2010 McLaren idea: the driver covered a hole in the cockpit to send air to the rear wing and stall it on straights. Banned from 2011, when DRS took over.
The Brabham BT46B of 1978, which used a large fan to suck air from under the car. It won its only race, in Sweden, and was withdrawn.
A spring-mounted weight inside the nose used by Renault in 2005–06 to steady the car over kerbs. Banned mid-2006.
Front-and-rear interconnected suspension, which kept the car level under braking and cornering. Banned in 2014.
Two ways of linking the wheels to the springs and dampers inside the car. Which one is used affects packaging and airflow.
The tilt of the tyres seen from the front. F1 cars run negative camber (tops leaning in) for cornering grip. Track camber is the slope of the road surface itself.
The angle of the wheels seen from above: toe-in points them toward each other, toe-out away. It affects stability and turn-in.
A test facility that blows air over a scale model (up to 60%) to measure downforce and drag. Time in it is limited by the rules.
Computational Fluid Dynamics: simulating airflow on computers. Limited by the rules alongside wind-tunnel time.
Aerodynamic Testing Restrictions: since 2021 teams get wind-tunnel and CFD time on a sliding scale, with the champion team getting the least.
A package of new parts (floor, wing, sidepods) brought to a race to make the car faster.

The complete F1 engine. In 2014–2025: a 1.6-litre V6 turbo (ICE) plus turbocharger, MGU-K, MGU-H, battery and control electronics. From 2026 the MGU-H is gone and the electric share is close to half of total power.
Internal combustion engine: the 1.6-litre turbocharged V6 at the heart of the power unit.
Energy Recovery System: the hybrid part of the power unit that harvests energy, stores it in the battery and deploys it as extra power.
Motor Generator Unit–Kinetic: an electric motor on the drivetrain that harvests energy under braking and gives it back as power. Up to 120 kW until 2025; 350 kW from 2026.
Motor Generator Unit–Heat: a generator on the turbocharger that harvested energy from exhaust heat and cut turbo lag. Used 2014–2025, dropped for 2026.
The lithium-ion battery that holds harvested electrical energy.
Kinetic Energy Recovery System: the first hybrid boost (2009, then 2011–2013), worth about 80 hp for under seven seconds a lap.

From 2026: a driver within one second of the car ahead at the detection point gets extra electrical energy (+0.5 MJ) to use on the next lap, and can keep full 350 kW deployment up to 337 km/h while other cars taper off from 290 km/h. Called Manual Override Mode (MOM) in early drafts.
A 2026 button the driver can press anywhere on the lap to deploy maximum electrical power, as long as there is energy in the battery.
The energy a car may harvest per lap under the 2026 rules (braking, lifting, part-throttle and super clipping). The allowance varies by circuit.
A 2026 technique: harvesting energy at the end of a straight while still flat on the throttle, so the car's speed tops out early.
When the battery stops deploying before the end of a straight, so the top speed flattens out or drops.
To use stored electrical energy for extra power.
To recover energy into the battery, mainly under braking.
The electronic rear brake system that blends normal hydraulic braking with the braking effect of the MGU-K harvesting energy.
How braking force is split between front and rear axles. Drivers adjust it corner by corner from the steering wheel.
Mercedes' name for a steering-wheel setting (2020) that shifted brake bias sharply forward to heat the front tyres behind the Safety Car.
The device that lets the rear wheels turn at different speeds through corners. Drivers tune it for corner entry, mid-corner and exit.
The slowing effect of the engine and energy recovery when lifting off and changing down, which also helps rotate the car into a corner.
A power-unit setting chosen from the steering wheel, from fuel-saving to maximum attack. Teams use code names on the radio.
Fan name for the maximum-power qualifying engine modes of the late 2010s. From late 2020 teams had to use the same mode in qualifying and the race.
Lifting off the throttle before the normal braking point and rolling into the corner to save fuel, cool the brakes or engine, or harvest energy.
From 2026 F1 cars run on fully sustainable fuel, made from non-fossil sources such as waste or captured carbon.
An eight-speed seamless-shift gearbox, changed with paddles behind the steering wheel in milliseconds.
Electronic systems that managed wheelspin at the start. Banned; drivers now control the clutch themselves with a paddle.
Electronics that cut power to stop wheelspin. Banned since 2008, when a standard ECU was introduced.
The FIA-standard electronic control unit every team must use, made by McLaren Applied, which polices driver aids.
The live stream of data from hundreds of sensors on the car to engineers in the garage and at the factory.
Packaging the engine and gearbox as tightly as possible for slimmer bodywork. Best known from McLaren-Honda's 2015 design.
Each driver may use only a set number of each power-unit component per season. Using more triggers grid penalties.
Official FIA approval that freezes a design, such as a power unit or crash structure, for a set period.
Pirelli's dry slick tyres run from C1 (hardest) to C6 (softest, added in 2025). Three are chosen for each race and marked Hard (white), Medium (yellow) and Soft (red).
The three dry compounds nominated for a race, with white, yellow and red sidewall markings. Softer means more grip and faster wear.
Green-marked treaded tyres for a damp track or light rain. At speed each tyre clears about 30 litres of water a second.
Blue-marked tyres for heavy rain, clearing about 85 litres of water a second per tyre at speed.
Dry tyres with no tread pattern, for maximum rubber on the road. Used since 1971, apart from the grooved-tyre years 1998–2008.
Dry tyres with four grooves (three on the front in 1998), used from 1998 to 2008 to cut grip and speeds.
In a dry race each driver must use at least two different dry compounds. It does not apply if wet or intermediate tyres are used.
Brand-new tyres, still with the manufacturer's stickers on.
Tyres that have been through one short heat cycle, such as an out-lap and in-lap, so they are no longer new.
Electric covers that heat tyres before they go on the car. Still allowed, at lower temperatures than in the past.
Loss of tyre performance over a stint, from heat as well as wear. A tyre can lose grip even with plenty of tread left.
Physical loss of rubber from the tread.
The moment a worn tyre suddenly loses its remaining grip, and lap times drop by seconds.
When the inside of a tyre overheats so much that rubber bubbles up and breaks away from the surface.
Small rolls of rubber that tear off a tyre sliding on a cool surface and stick back onto the tread, cutting grip until they wear away.
A flat patch ground into a tyre when a wheel locks under braking. It makes the car vibrate badly.
When a wheel stops turning under braking and slides, often with blue smoke from the tyre.
Small balls of discarded rubber that collect off the racing line. Running over them feels like driving on ice.
Driving over marbles on the slowing-down lap to collect rubber, sometimes to help the car meet the minimum weight.
The small area of each tyre actually touching the road at any moment.
Pirelli sets minimum starting pressures for each race, which the FIA checks.
One warm-up and cool-down of a tyre. Each cycle changes the rubber slightly.
A tyre outside its working temperature range: too cold to grip, or too hot and degrading.
A track with little rubber laid down, such as on Friday morning or after rain, which feels slippery.
The track getting faster as rubber is laid down and dust blown away during a session or weekend.
The front tyres run out of grip first, so the car will not turn enough and runs wide.
The rear tyres run out of grip first, so the back of the car slides.
A sudden, violent loss of rear grip that needs instant opposite lock to save.
Steering against a slide to catch an oversteering car.
When a tyre rides on a layer of standing water and loses contact with the road.
How evenly grip is shared between front and rear. Drivers adjust it with front-wing angle and settings on the steering wheel.
Grip and response from the front end on turn-in.
The innermost point a driver aims for in a corner.
The fastest path around a circuit.
A slower car at the back of the field, often about to be lapped.
A very late-braking lunge down the inside from a long way back.
Committing fully to a risky move.
Licking the stamp and sending it
Daniel Ricciardo's phrase for committing to a late-braking pass.
Braking later than the driver alongside to take the corner first.
Letting a rival go into a corner first, then turning back underneath them for a better exit.
Pushing a rival toward the edge of the track to make them back off.
Giving a rival who is alongside enough room. Not doing so can bring a penalty.
Changing line in the braking zone, which is dangerous and can be penalised.
Zig-zagging on the straight to break a slipstream or block. Only one defensive move is allowed.
A defending driver may make one change of direction to defend a position.
Protecting a position by taking the inside line into corners.
Two cars racing side by side.
A queue of cars each within a second of the one ahead, so all have DRS and nobody can pass.
A queue of faster cars stuck behind a slower one, after Jarno Trulli, who often held up the field this way.
Pitting before the car ahead to use the speed of new tyres and be in front when they stop.
Staying out longer than a rival who has pitted, using clear air to stay ahead after your own stop.
The range of laps when a planned stop makes most sense.
A gap to the car behind big enough to pit without losing a place, roughly the time a stop costs (about 20–25 seconds at most tracks).
The time a pit stop costs compared with staying out.
Pitting both team cars on the same lap, one behind the other.
How many pit stops a strategy plans.
The laps run on one set of tyres.
Being ahead on the road, which matters most where overtaking is hard.
The difference in tyre age or compound between two cars.
Gap is the time to the leader; interval is the time to the car directly ahead.
A time difference, such as between laps or between two cars. Under a VSC drivers must stay above a minimum delta time.
A car's speed. Quali pace is one-lap speed; race pace is speed over a long run.
A practice run of many laps on heavy fuel to test race pace and tyre wear.
The lap from the pit lane, used to warm tyres before a flying lap or race stint.
The lap ending with a pit stop.
The slow lap after the chequered flag or a fast run.
A tight left-right or right-left pair of corners that slows the cars down.
Painted, ridged strips on the edges of corners. Taller sausage kerbs stop drivers cutting corners.
The white lines at the edge of the track. Going beyond them with all four wheels can lose a lap time or bring a penalty.
The area beyond the track edge, made of gravel, grass or asphalt.
A bed of gravel beyond a corner to slow a car that goes off.
A corner where the track slopes away from the inside, pushing cars outward. Positive camber or banking does the opposite.
A commentators' line for two cars trying to take the same piece of track and colliding.
A collision the stewards decide was nobody's fault, with no penalty.
Instructions from the team for one driver to let the other past or hold position. Legal again since 2011.
A strategy call: if the car ahead pits, stay out; if it stays out, pit.
Practice sessions on Friday (and Saturday at non-sprint weekends) with no points at stake: FP1, FP2 and FP3.
The session that sets the grid, in three knockout parts: Q1, Q2 and Q3.
The three knockout parts of qualifying, used since 2006. The slowest cars drop out of Q1 and Q2 (six each with 22 cars from 2026), and the top ten fight for pole in Q3.
A driver slower than 107% of the fastest Q1 time may not start the race unless the stewards allow it.
First place on the starting grid, earned by the fastest qualifier.
The first two places on the grid.
A short Saturday race of about 100 km with points for the top eight (8 down to 1), held at six weekends a season.
The short qualifying session that sets the sprint grid.
The lap before the start, behind the pole sitter, to warm tyres and brakes.
The starting positions in two staggered lines.
The usual F1 start from a stationary grid.
A start while moving, behind the Safety Car, used in very wet conditions.
The start of a race, when the five red lights go out.
Lights out and away we go
Moving before the lights go out, which brings a penalty.
The black-and-white flag that ends a race or session.
Finishing or running positions: P1 is first place.
Did Not Finish, Did Not Start, Disqualified.
A driver who completes at least 90% of the winner's distance counts as a finisher, even if he stopped.
The top three finishers, and the stage where they receive trophies.
25-18-15-12-10-8-6-4-2-1 for the top ten in a Grand Prix. A point for fastest lap was given from 2019 to 2024.
The quickest lap of the race. It earned a bonus point (if in the top ten) from 2019 to 2024.
How ties in the championship are broken: most wins, then most second places, and so on.
The world title for the driver with the most points over the season.
The title for the team with the most points from both cars.
Pole position, race win and fastest lap at the same Grand Prix.
Pole, win, fastest lap and leading every lap. Jim Clark holds the record with eight.
A fan vote after each race.
The few days of official testing before the first race.
A short first run of a new car to check it works. Filming days are limited to 200 km on special tyres.
Hiding a car's real speed in testing or practice with heavy fuel or low engine modes.
A driver in his first F1 season. Teams must give FP1 sessions to rookies twice a year per car.
Fédération Internationale de l'Automobile, the body that governs F1 and writes its rules.
The panel of officials, including an ex-driver, who judge incidents and give penalties.
The FIA official who runs the race: starts, flags, Safety Cars and red flags.
Track clear, or the start of a session.
Danger ahead: slow down, no overtaking. Double waved yellows mean be ready to stop.
Session or race stopped. All cars return slowly to the pit lane.
Shown to a car about to be lapped: let the faster car through. Ignoring three in a row brings a penalty.
The driver is disqualified and must return to the pits.
A car has dangerous damage and must pit to have it fixed.
A warning for unsporting behaviour or repeated track-limits offences, like a yellow card.
Slippery surface ahead: oil, water or debris.
Slow vehicle ahead, such as a recovery truck or a damaged car.
A road car that leads the field at reduced speed after an incident. Overtaking is banned.
Every driver slows to a set delta time without a physical Safety Car, which keeps the gaps roughly the same.
Lapped cars overtaking the leaders behind the Safety Car to rejoin the lead lap before a restart.
A painted line after which the Safety Car rules end and racing resumes.
From qualifying until the race, most of the car's setup cannot be changed without starting from the pit lane.
Technical checks by the FIA to make sure cars meet the rules.
The lowest weight a car (with driver) may be. 800 kg until 2025, 768 kg from 2026.
Time added at the next pit stop (before work starts) or to the race time.
A penalty where the driver must drive through the pit lane at the speed limit.
A penalty where the driver stops in his box for 10 seconds with no work done.
A driver starting a set number of places back, often for using extra power-unit parts.
A penalty that puts a driver at the rear of the grid.
Points on a driver's superlicence for driving offences. Twelve within 12 months brings a one-race ban.
A formal warning. Five in a season (at least four for driving) bring a grid penalty.
The licence needed to race in F1, earned with points from junior series.
Sending a car out of its pit box into another car's path.
Usually 80 km/h in the pit lane, enforced by a limiter button.
A team can ask the stewards to look again at a decision when there is significant new evidence.
The yearly limit on what a team may spend on car performance. US$135 million (base) for 2023–2025; US$215 million from 2026, when more costs came under it. Driver salaries are excluded.
The contract between teams, the FIA and Formula One Management covering prize money and governance.
Formula One Management, the commercial rights holder, owned by Liberty Media.
The radio call telling a driver to pit this lap. From German Boxenstopp, pit stop.
Cancel the pit stop and stay on track.
Pre-planned race strategies. Ferrari's 'Plan E' and 'We are checking' became fan jokes.
Mercedes' call to Lewis Hamilton to push as hard as possible.
Lewis Hamilton to his race engineer Peter Bonnington, often just before setting fast laps.
Red Bull's 2013 Malaysian GP code for 'car 2 ahead of car 1': Webber ahead of Vettel. Vettel ignored it and won.
Max Verstappen's signature celebration on the radio.
Carlos Sainz's song on the radio after good results.
Leave me alone, I know what I'm doing
Kimi Räikkönen to his engineer on the way to winning the 2012 Abu Dhabi GP.
Fernando Alonso's 2015 Japanese GP complaint about the Honda power unit.
A fan meme built around Fernando Alonso's 'master plan'.
A common driver radio complaint meant for the stewards.
The tyres have no grip left.
Lights out and away we go
David Croft's signature start call on Sky Sports F1.
The covered stand on the pit straight where the team principal, strategists and engineers watch the race.
The engineer who speaks to the driver on the radio and runs the car's setup.
The person in charge of a team at races and overall.
The team manager who deals with rules, the FIA and race procedures.
About 20 mechanics who change tyres in a stop: wheel-gun operators, tyre on and off, front and rear jacks.
Stopping in the pit box to change tyres or fix damage. The record is 1.80 seconds by McLaren (Norris, Qatar 2023).
The sign once used to tell a driver to go; now mostly replaced by lights.
The mechanic who lifts the front or rear of the car.
The air gun that removes and fits the single wheel nut.
The team's working space in the pit building.
The private area behind the garages with team motorhomes, hospitality and offices.
The premium hospitality suites above the garages.
The team's temporary building in the paddock for meals, meetings and media.
A driver ready to step in if a race driver cannot race.
A full-size driving rig at the factory used to prepare setups and learn tracks.
A team run by a car or engine maker.
A team that buys its power unit, and sometimes other parts, from another team.
A team's academy for young drivers on their way to F1.
The months of driver-market rumours and seat changes.
A driver whose seat depends largely on money brought from sponsors or family.
The broadcast walk among the cars on the grid before the start, made famous by Martin Brundle.
The area where drivers give interviews after sessions.
A lap of the circuit before the race when drivers wave to fans.
Drivers and engineers walking the circuit on Thursday to study it.
Ferrari's passionate fans. Italian for 'fans', from tifo, a word linked to typhus fever.
Max Verstappen's Dutch fans, in orange.
Drinking champagne from a racing boot on the podium, made famous in F1 by Daniel Ricciardo.
Netflix's F1 documentary series (from 2019), credited with a big rise in new fans.
McLaren's guidelines for letting its drivers race each other fairly, from 2024.
Slang for a slow, uncompetitive car.
Fan nickname for Sergio Pérez after his defence against Hamilton at the 2021 Abu Dhabi GP.
Fan nickname for George Russell's qualifying speed.
The 2008 Singapore GP scandal: Renault ordered Nelson Piquet Jr. to crash to bring out a Safety Car that helped Fernando Alonso win.
The 2007 scandal in which McLaren held Ferrari technical data. McLaren was fined US$100 million and lost its constructors' points.
The pass that gets you into the paddock.
An amateur who raced on private money, common in early F1.
1977–1988, when turbocharged engines produced over 1,000 hp in qualifying. Turbos were banned from 1989 and returned in 2014.
Naturally aspirated V10s ran from 1995 to 2005, then 2.4-litre V8s until 2013.
From 2014: turbo hybrid power units with energy recovery.
Topping up fuel during pit stops, allowed 1994–2009 and banned since 2010.
Periods when two tyre makers competed in F1, notably Bridgestone and Michelin from 2001 to 2006. Single supplier since 2007, Pirelli since 2011.
The Tyrrell P34 of 1976–77, with four small front wheels. It won the 1976 Swedish GP.
Skirts on ground-effect cars that slid down to seal the floor to the track. Banned in 1981.
Part of the World Championship from 1950 to 1960, though few F1 regulars took part.
The front of the chassis that carries the front wing and contains a crash structure tested in impact tests.
A front-suspension layout of the 2000s in which the lower wishbones met under a raised nose with no keel beneath it, freeing airflow under the car.
Where a driver will be once everyone has made the same number of pit stops.
How air flows over and under the car. In F1 it is about creating downforce for grip while keeping drag low.
The opening above the driver's head that feeds air to the engine (and in older cars a tall airbox).
The car's outer carbon panels: engine cover, sidepods, nose and so on.
The wing at the back that produces rear downforce. Its flap opened for DRS until 2025 and moves with active aero from 2026.
The distance between the front and rear axles. Limited to 3.6 m until 2025 and 3.4 m from 2026.
Strong, light woven carbon material set in resin, used for almost the whole car since McLaren's MP4/1 of 1981.
The main structure of the car, built around the monocoque, to which engine and suspension are attached. 'Constructor' means the team that builds it.
The space where the driver sits.
The springs, dampers and wishbones joining the wheels to the car, set up to control grip and ride height.
A suspension part (also called a J-damper) that helped control tyre bounce. Banned from 2022.
A small wing mounted on top of the engine cover in 2017, banned for 2018.
A vertical fin on the engine cover to steady airflow to the rear wing, used in various years.
Tall wings mounted on stalks directly to the suspension in 1968–69. Several broke and caused crashes, so they were banned mid-1969.
A flat floor between the wheels, required from 1983 to 2021 to limit ground-effect downforce.
Mercedes' 2020 system that changed the front wheels' toe when the driver pushed or pulled the steering wheel. Banned from 2021.
Any part shaped to change airflow. The 2009 and 2022 rules removed many of them to make following easier.
Computer-controlled suspension that kept the car at the ideal height. Williams dominated with it in 1992–93; banned for 1994.
Anti-lock brakes, which stop wheels locking under braking. Banned since 1994.
Continuously variable transmission: a gearbox with no fixed gears, tested by Williams in 1993 and banned before it raced.
An engine that breathes air at normal pressure, without a turbo or supercharger.
A compressor driven by the engine itself that forces more air in for more power. Allowed in early F1 (also called a compressor).
A compressor driven by exhaust gas that forces extra air into the engine. Used 1977–1988 and again since 2014.
How hard the turbo pushes air into the engine, in bar. Limited to 4.0 bar in 1987 and 2.5 bar in 1988 before turbos were banned.
The total volume of the engine's cylinders, in litres or cc (cubic centimetres). 1.6 litres = 1600 cc. A bigger capacity usually means more power.
The chambers where fuel burns. V6, V8, V10 and V12 mean six, eight, ten or twelve cylinders arranged in a V shape.
The maximum engine speed allowed: 19,000 rpm in 2007, 18,000 rpm 2009–2013, and 15,000 rpm in the hybrid era.
A rule stopping makers from developing their engines, used from 2007 and in the hybrid era, to cut costs.
From 2014 to 2017, a limited number of 'tokens' each power-unit maker could spend on upgrades.
The 3-litre V8 that Ford funded and Cosworth built in 1967. Cheap and widely available, it won 155 races into the 1980s.
A car with the engine behind the driver. Cooper's success in 1959–60 made it the standard layout.
The power unit's electronic brain, managing energy flow between battery, motor and engine.
The flexible, puncture-resistant fuel tank inside the monocoque.
The twisting force an engine delivers, which drives acceleration out of corners.
The grip the rear tyres have under acceleration.
How well the tyres hold the road. It comes from the tyres themselves (mechanical grip) and from downforce (aerodynamic grip).
How a car behaves through corners: balance, response and stability.
Tyres below their working temperature, with little grip, common on out-laps and restarts.
The temperature of the asphalt, which strongly affects tyre grip and wear.
Older names (2007–2010s) for the softer (option) and harder (prime) of the two dry compounds at a race.
Cars leaving rubber on the racing line, which adds grip over a session.
A sequence of quick left-right-left corners, like the S in their name.
The spot where a driver starts braking for a corner.
Braking with the left foot while the right stays on the throttle; standard in F1 since cars lost clutch pedals.
A controlled slide with the rear tyres sliding.
When the engine cuts out, most often at the start.
A timing point on the fastest straight that records top speed.
Each lap is split into three timed sectors.
The fastest race lap ever set on a circuit's current layout.
A car the leader has passed a full lap ahead of.
The force drivers feel in braking, cornering and acceleration, up to about 5–6 g in F1.
A race held after dark under floodlights, first at Singapore in 2008.
A short lap at the start of a session to check that the car works.
A lap from the pit lane to the grid before the race, used to check conditions.
Stopping during a race because of damage, a fault or a crash.
Did Not Qualify: too slow to make the grid, common when more cars entered than could start.
French for 'great prize': the name for each championship race.
The most important Grands Prix of the 1920s–40s. Before 1950 there was no championship; these races carried the prestige.
The junior single-seater class. In 1952 and 1953 the World Championship was run to its rules (2-litre engines) to get more cars on the grid.
From 1958 cars had to run on fuel close to aviation petrol instead of alcohol mixtures. Fuel today must be close to road fuel, and sustainable from 2026.
Until 1990 only a driver's best results counted toward the title, so some points were dropped.
In 2014 only, the final race awarded double points.
A 2005 format adding together times from two sessions. Dropped mid-season.
2003–2005: each driver ran one timed lap alone on track.
Wire fences once used to slow cars that left the track. Banned in 1986 because they caused injuries.
Impact tests every chassis must pass before racing: front from 1985, side and rear later.
The strong hoop above the driver's head that protects him if the car flips.
